headline: Sukuk trade below their own issuer's conventional curve
number: -18.6bp average across 18 issuers (median -8.7bp); 16 of 18 negative; 8 of 8 obligor groups negative on average (issuers grouped by the government backing them; Sharjah and the multilateral Arab Energy Fund stand alone).
interpretation: Holding the issuer fixed, investors accept a lower yield on sukuk.

headline: The sukuk premium is concentrated in the two governments rated sub-investment grade, Bahrain and Oman
number: By rating at the time (2 of 3 agencies below BBB-/Baa3; Dubai via its DEWA proxy), sub-IG obligor-months average -68bp vs -9bp for investment grade: gap -58bp, wild bootstrap p = 0.038 by obligor group. Robustness: without Dubai -56bp (p = 0.074); without Sharjah -62bp (p = 0.007); lowest rating -54bp (p = 0.013); government CDS above 150bp -55bp (p = 0.077); export-date snapshot ratings -45bp (p = 0.015). Oman's sukuk premium narrowed by 21bp (90% CI [10.3, 32.4]) in the year after Moody's upgrade made it investment grade at two of three agencies. Only two governments are ever sub-IG: the gap is -54bp without Bahrain (p = 0.308) and -60bp without Oman (p = 0.181), and against all 21 pairs of governments the permutation p is 0.048, the lowest that test can give. The gap falls from -76bp before 2021 to -37bp from 2023 (p = 0.139).
interpretation: Concentrated, not exclusive: Sharjah (-44bp) counts as investment grade under the rule because it is split rated and Fitch does not rate it, yet its premium looks like the sub-IG group's and predates Moody's 2022 cut. The rating line approximates what investors price; it is not a sharp threshold. Two sub-IG governments cannot separate sub-IG status from other features of Bahrain and Oman.

headline: Within the weakest sovereigns, the sukuk premium moves with credit risk
number: Oman -21.5bp and Bahrain -19.2bp per 100bp of CDS (Newey-West t -4.0, -3.0); also in monthly changes (-50.0, -21.2). By rating at the time, the within slope is +10.4bp in investment-grade months and -35.0bp lower in sub-IG months (p = 0.038).
interpretation: The pooled panel slope (-22.0bp) is not significant on its own once only six CDS series are counted (wild bootstrap p = 0.287); the case studies carry the claim.

headline: The sukuk premium exists at issue, not only in secondary quotes
number: Classifying each deal by its government's rating at pricing (MAIN rule: two of three agencies below BBB-/Baa3), weak-credit sukuk priced through their issuer's conventional curve: median new-issue premium -55.2bp (n = 15), vs +18.6bp for weak-credit conventional deals, which came with the ordinary concession (n = 23), and -3.0bp for other issuers' sukuk: a sukuk-minus-conventional gap of -73.9bp (robustness range -65.8 to -42.1bp). Issuer-level correlation with the secondary basis 0.78.
interpretation: Stale secondary quotes cannot explain a premium that is already there on the pricing date. Under MAIN almost all weak-credit sukuk are Bahraini (14 of 15); the lowest-rating and spread rules, which keep more non-Bahraini deals, give the same sign without Bahrain.

headline: Sukuk quotes are somewhat stale, but that is not the story
number: Unchanged mid price on 7.9% of days for sukuk vs 1.5% for conventionals; sukuk absorb 0.47 of a conventional move on the day and 0.62 within a week (weak credits 0.56, KSA 0.89); 46% of the pooled same-month CDS effect reverses within six months (Bahrain: no reversal).
interpretation: Even after 120 business days sukuk move 0.83bp per conventional bp: damping is real, and stale quotes explain only part of the monthly CDS response.

headline: Mechanism: tenor and buy-and-hold demand, with modest evidence
number: Holm-adjusted p-values across the four mechanism tests (government-clustered wild bootstrap): CDS slope steepens by -2.1bp per 100bp per year of maturity (p 0.138); less liquid sukuk price richer, -0.81bp per bp of bid-ask gap (p 0.076); CDS x interbank spread -0.10 per bp (p 0.626); CDS x Ijara +10.9 (p 0.718), a low-power test because only 10 of the 68 twin sukuk are Ijara (43 are Hybrid).
interpretation: After the multiple-testing correction none clears 5%; the tenor and liquidity signs fit default/recovery pricing plus buy-and-hold demand. The Ijara test cannot rule asset backing in or out.

headline: Oil shocks do not move the basis directly
number: Median basis response to an oil-price rise +0.6bp at +5 days; the test could detect 3.1bp (+5) or 4.9bp (+20) with 80% power. Implied via credit: +0.71bp (90% CI [-0.82, 2.77]).
interpretation: Oil reaches the basis only through credit risk, and oil up-shocks in this sample raise GCC CDS (median +5.9bp at +5 days, placebo p < 0.001); several of them are regional conflicts.

headline: What it is worth
number: Bahrain about USD 45m a year; Sharjah about USD 27m a year; BAPCO Energies BSCC Closed about USD 11m a year (trailing-12-month basis x outstanding USD sukuk). Investment-grade sovereigns without USD sukuk (Kuwait, Abu Dhabi, UAE federal): predicted USD 0.3-1.3m per USD 1bn issued, intervals including zero.
interpretation: Sukuk issuance pays most for the weakest credits, which is where the premium sits.
